title: Why position matters
summary: Playing in and out of position, and why ranges widen towards the button.

info.text:
The player who acts last is **in position**. They see what their opponents did before deciding. That gives them:
- **Information**: a check often means weakness, a bet strength.
- **Pot control**: they can check behind and see the next card for free.
- **Better bluffs**: when the opponent checks, a bet often takes the pot.
- **More of their equity turns into chips**: they are forced to fold less often.

behind.text: The second reason is **how many players are behind you**. From UTG five opponents still act, and one of them may hold a strong hand. From the button only the blinds remain, and you will be in position after the flop. That's why players open about 14% of hands from UTG and 40% or more from the button.

utg.caption: Open-raise from UTG: strong hands only.

btn.caption: Open-raise from the button: several times wider.

oop.text:
Playing **out of position** is harder: you act first without knowing what your opponent will do. So out of position you play fewer hands, lead or check-raise more, and fold marginal hands more often.

This is also why the blinds are the worst seats: after the flop they almost always act first.

q-wider.q: Why do players open more hands from the button than from UTG?
options: Fewer players are left behind, and you are in position after the flop
q-wider.explain: Fewer opponents behind means less chance to run into a strong hand. Position after the flop helps you play medium hands too.

t1.q: What does being in position mean?
t1.explain: In position you act after your opponent and see their decision first.

t2.q: Which 6-max seat is best after the flop?
t2.explain: The button acts last on the flop, turn and river against anyone.

t3.q: How should you play out of position?
options: Wider, to make up for it
Tighter, folding marginal hands more often
t3.explain: Out of position you have less information and keep less of your equity, so you choose hands more strictly.
